strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse datasets (real-world and synthetic) with thorough ablation studies demonstrating the contribution of each component
Strong empirical results on multi-class tasks with extreme bias ratios (e.g., 89.02% vs 83.20% on cMNIST at 0.5% bias-conflicting ratio)
Clear identification of CCDB's limitations (single Gaussian approximation) and principled fine-grained solution with practical advantages (closed-form computation, negligible memory overhead)
Well-designed validation of bias prediction quality against ground-truth annotations with analysis of the effect of repeating the bias enhancement learning procedure
Effective visualizations and clear presentation demonstrating the practical utility of the approach through feature correlation analysis and weight distribution analysis
weaknesses: Limited novelty: BEO applies straightforward techniques (random splitting, selecting high-confidence samples) without introducing fundamentally new insights; FG-CCDB is a natural extension of CCDB using predicted groups rather than a novel algorithmic contribution

Restrictive and unjustified assumptions: The |Y| = |S| assumption (one bias attribute per class) is limiting and frequently violated in practice; the paper acknowledges this causes failures on CelebA and CivilComments but provides no solutions or detailed analysis

Weak theoretical justification: No theoretical analysis of why selecting top-50% confidence samples improves bias prediction; the connection between distribution matching (Eq. 1) and practical weight computation (Eqs. 2-4) is not rigorously justified; no convergence guarantees or approximation quality analysis

Modest improvements on real-world binary classification tasks: Waterbirds worst-group 90.56 vs 90.48 (CCDB) is within noise; CivilComments shows gains but improvements are often only 1-3% on real-world datasets where the practical benefit is limited

Insufficient analysis of BEO limitations: No sensitivity analysis for key design choices (γ = 10%, 50% confidence threshold); acknowledged failures on datasets deviating from typical spurious correlation patterns lack characterization or solutions; hyperparameter choices lack principled justification

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem of group-robust classification without bias annotations
Clear and intuitive two-stage BEO methodology with efficient closed-form solutions for sample reweighting
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple real-world and synthetic datasets with thorough ablation studies
Demonstrates strong performance improvements on multi-class synthetic datasets (cMNIST: +5.82% over CCDB at 0.5% bias)
Provides detailed analysis of bias prediction quality, sample weight distributions, and component contributions
weaknesses: Limited novelty: BEO is a straightforward confidence-based filtering approach, and FG-CCDB is an incremental extension of CCDB with group-level rather than class-level matching
Marginal real-world improvements over CCDB baseline—often within error margins (Waterbirds: 90.56% vs 90.48%; CelebA i.i.d.: actually worse at 89.71% vs 90.08%)
Restrictive core assumption |Y|=|S| (single dominant bias per class) is violated on tested datasets (acknowledged for CelebA and CivilComments), with no robustness analysis to assumption violations
BEO reliability concerns: Group prediction accuracy plateaus at ~85-90% (Figure 4), and the claimed 'strong proxy for ground-truth annotations' is overstated given imperfect predictions

Unjustified methodological choices: 50% threshold for sample selection lacks ablation; model selection via worst-class accuracy on validation without ground-truth group labels is unclear; Equation 3 lacks theoretical justification
Missing critical analysis: No computational cost comparison, sensitivity analysis for γ parameter, or explanation of why CCDB/SELF surpass supervised methods on CivilComments by large margins
Limited experimental scope: No controlled experiments deliberately violating core assumptions; only image and text domains; heterogeneous hyperparameters across datasets suggest tuning sensitivity

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 diverse datasets (real-world binary and synthetic multi-class) with multiple baseline comparisons and ablation studies demonstrating each component's contribution
Strong empirical results consistently achieving competitive or superior worst-group accuracy compared to bias-supervised methods, particularly on multi-class tasks (98.21% on cMNIST vs CCDB 96.37%)
Technically sound and practical design with elegant closed-form sample weight computation (Eqs. 2-4) that avoids storing per-sample feature representations, providing computational efficiency

Well-motivated problem addressing annotation-free group-robust classification with clear presentation and concrete motivation; demonstrates BEO can serve as reasonable substitute for human annotations

Clear technical contributions combining overfitting-based bias discovery with fine-grained distribution matching, showing good performance across diverse domains without requiring validation-time bias annotations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: BEO is essentially two-stage confidence-based filtering building on prior work (SELF, LfF), and FG-CCDB is a straightforward extension of CCDB replacing single Gaussians with group-level quantization
Restrictive assumption |Y| = |S| (one bias attribute per class) significantly limits real-world applicability; paper acknowledges failure cases (CelebA, CivilComments) without providing solutions

Critical design choices lack justification: γ=10% and 50% confidence threshold chosen without ablation studies or sensitivity analysis; default 3 iterations despite Figure 4 showing plateau after 1 iteration

Lack of theoretical foundation: no analysis of when/why BEO succeeds or fails, why two-stage overfitting outperforms alternatives theoretically, or conditions for exact distribution matching (Eq. 3) with estimated distributions

Performance trade-offs not adequately addressed: FG-CCDB occasionally underperforms CCDB on i.i.d. accuracy (Waterbirds 92.50% vs 92.59%, CelebA 89.71% vs 90.08%), suggesting overfitting to worst-group scenarios without discussion
BEO as 'annotation substitute' shows non-trivial gaps to ground truth (GroupDRO-BEO 88.47% vs GroupDRO 91.40% on Waterbirds, ~3% gap), raising questions about claims in abstract

Missing analysis: no ablation on 50% threshold, no robustness analysis for extreme imbalances, no runtime/computational cost comparison despite 'lightweight' claims, potential numerical instability in Eq. 4 with small groups
Reproducibility concerns: Algorithm 1 lacks implementation details on pseudo-bias label usage, CCDB baseline from 2025 arXiv raises novelty concerns, limited hyperparameter sensitivity analysis

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse datasets and settings (binary/multi-class, single/multiple shortcuts) with proper methodology (5 seeds, fair splits, extensive baselines)
Strong empirical results particularly on challenging multi-class and multi-shortcut scenarios (e.g., 89.02% vs 83.20% on cMNIST at 0.5% bias ratio), demonstrating practical value
Well-motivated refinement of CCDB with concrete solution to Gaussian approximation limitation through mode-level distribution matching
Thorough analysis including bias prediction quality evaluation (F1-score/precision/recall), feature correlation shifts, ablations, and hyperparameter sensitivity
Practical advantages: closed-form weight computation, negligible memory overhead, integrable with existing bias-supervised methods, requires no bias annotations
Detailed experimental methodology and extensive appendix addressing potential concerns and design choices
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution is replacing Gaussian approximation with mode-level approximation (relatively straightforward); MST uses confidence-based filtering, an established technique; primarily incremental over CCDB

Weak theoretical justification: no analysis of approximation quality gains, convergence guarantees for MST, or principled justification for intra-mode homogeneity assumption; EOF connection appears post-hoc

Structural limitations acknowledged but unresolved: method depends critically on ERM overfitting to bias cues, which fails when this signal is weak (CelebA: 51.72% bias-aligned ratio, CivilComments). This is not peripheral—it's a fundamental limitation

Hyperparameter choices lack principled justification: β=50% justified by 'bias-aligned ratio typically >50%' is somewhat circular (CelebA violates this); γ=10% lacks theoretical motivation; adaptive β sometimes performs better (Table 8), suggesting fixed choices suboptimal

Incremental improvements on standard benchmarks: Table 1 binary classification with single shortcut shows overlapping confidence intervals (Waterbirds: 92.50±0.52 vs 92.59±0.10); CelebA i.i.d. performance actually slightly worse; main gains only on synthetic multi-class datasets

Gap between FG-CCDB-sup and FG-CCDB indicates sensitivity to mode prediction quality: CelebA shows 93.14±0.16 vs 89.71±0.54 (3.4% drop); claim about compensation for imperfect partitions lacks detailed analysis

Circular definition of bias: using predicted bias from auxiliary overfitted model to define modes used for debiasing; quality directly depends on overfitting signal, creating dependency on the very phenomenon MST aims to correct

Presentation and design choices: 'mode' terminology obscures comparison with group-based methods; important design choices (intra-mode homogeneity, entropy-based subdivision failure) relegated to appendix; computational overhead (0.27-1.26h) deserves prominent discussion
